source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Diagnosis (artificial intelligence), model-based diagnosis section
finding: Model-based diagnosis is described as abductive reasoning with a model. Simulate the model, compare predicted with observed behaviour. Two rules use an abnormal predicate: not Ab(S) implies normal internal and observable behaviour; Ab(S) implies fault-model behaviour. Given the observations, decide Ab(S) or not Ab(S).
numbers: Rules: ~Ab(S) => Int1 & Obs1; Ab(S) => Int2 & Obs2 (fault model). Cites Hamscher, Console, de Kleer (1992) Readings in Model-Based Diagnosis. DX workshops since 1989.
limits: Encyclopedia page, no experiments. Says the faulty model is often little known, so the model can be incomplete. Fetched raw wikitext and read the section.
agent_relevance: O8 reframe: write the expected normal behaviour as an explicit model, mark each part with an Ab flag, and compare predicted to observed output to localise the part that is wrong.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Model-based reasoning
finding: Model-based reasoning means an engine combines a model of the physical world with observed data to reach a diagnosis or prediction. Builders focus on the model, not on rules. Brooks (1990) and the nouvelle AI school criticised symbolic models as detached from physical systems.
numbers: Causal rule Stroke -> Confused & UnequalPupils versus diagnostic rules Confused -> Stroke. Layered design since the 1990s: model layer (monitor, evaluate) and control layer (choose actions). Models may be quantitative or qualitative and may cover only abnormal behaviour.
limits: Article does not discuss the Ab predicate or abductive diagnosis (checked). Thin source.
agent_relevance: Gives the causal versus diagnostic direction: abduction runs the causal model backward from observed effects to causes. Keep the forward model separate from the backward search.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Abductive reasoning, logic-based and set-cover sections
finding: Logic-based abduction: given theory T and observations O, find explanation E with T plus E entails O and T plus E consistent. A minimality condition is usually added because many E qualify. Selection uses simplicity, prior probability or explanatory power. Set-cover abduction: find a subset H' of hypotheses whose effects cover all manifestations M.
numbers: Two conditions: T u E |= O and T u E consistent. Abductive logic programs split T into a normal program (generates candidates by backward reasoning) and integrity constraints (filter them). Bi-abduction in the Infer tool scaled to millions of lines of code. Internist-I cited as a diagnostic abductive system.
quote: The most direct application of abduction is that of automatically detecting faults in systems
limits: Only the first 100000 of 159634 characters were read. Page does not use the term parsimonious covering.
agent_relevance: Gives two formal tests code can run on any proposed cause: does it entail every observation, and is it consistent with known facts. Supports a minimality filter on candidates.

source: Bhagavatula et al. (2020, ICLR; arXiv 2019) Abductive Commonsense Reasoning (ART, aNLI, aNLG)
finding: First large benchmark for abductive reasoning in language: given two observations O1 and O2, pick or generate the most plausible hypothesis. Adversarial filtering with BERT made pairs hard. Pre-trained models stayed far below humans.
numbers: ART: over 20k narrative contexts and 200k explanations. Best BERT-ft (fully connected) 68.9 percent on test, GPT-ft 63.1, majority 50.4, human 91.4 percent. Ablations on ART: BERT [O1 only] 63.5, [O2 only] 66.6, [hypothesis only] 59.5.
limits: 2019 models only. Two-choice format gives 50 percent chance. Hypotheses are short commonsense sentences, not systems with components.
agent_relevance: Baseline for what explaining from observations costs a plain model. Observation-only ablations scoring 63 to 67 show surface cues carry much of the score, so checks must use a held-out observation (G3).

source: Bhagavatula et al. (2020) ART, human upper bound
finding: Humans reach 91.4 percent on the test set; the gap to the best model is 22.5 points. The authors say models struggle on the abductive step even though they do well on entailment tasks.
numbers: 91.4 minus 68.9 = 22.5 points. A GPT adversary and a BERT adversary gave similar drops across all models.
limits: Human figure is for the two-choice task only.
agent_relevance: A measured gap on picking among given hypotheses. Generating hypotheses from scratch is harder (see the survey lines below).

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles, Artificial Intelligence 32(1):57-95
finding: Defines a system as (SD, COMP, OBS). A diagnosis is a minimal set Delta of components such that assuming Ab for Delta and not-Ab for all others is consistent with SD and OBS. Diagnoses are the minimal hitting sets of the conflict sets. This is the consistency-based form; it needs no fault models.
numbers: Theorem (from memory): Delta is a diagnosis iff it is a minimal hitting set of the collection of conflict sets. HS-tree algorithm computes them.
limits: From memory, not opened (publisher page returned 403). Overlaps C09 subfields 01 and 04, so only cited here.
agent_relevance: The Ab-flag formalism is implementable: a candidate fault set is accepted only if the model, with those parts set abnormal, reproduces what was seen.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults, Artificial Intelligence 32(1):97-130 (GDE)
finding: General Diagnostic Engine. Uses an ATMS to record minimal conflicts from predictions that clash with measurements, then forms minimal candidates. Ranks candidates by prior failure probability and proposes the next measurement that minimises expected entropy of the candidate distribution.
numbers: Component priors assumed independent; candidate probability is the product of fault probabilities and (1 - p) for the rest. Entropy-based probe choice (from memory).
limits: From memory, not opened. Pure consistency-based GDE can accept weak diagnoses unless fault models are added (Sherlock, de Kleer and Williams 1989).
agent_relevance: Maps to S5 (locate fault) and S7 (pick the next test): conflicts from failed predictions, then choose the probe that best splits remaining suspects.

source: de Kleer, Mackworth, Reiter (1992) Characterizing diagnoses and systems, Artificial Intelligence 56(2-3):197-222
finding: Unifies the Reiter and de Kleer-Williams views. Introduces kernel diagnoses and relates minimal diagnoses to minimal conflicts. Treats consistency-based diagnosis as the base and explains when fault models are needed.
numbers: No figures recalled with confidence.
limits: From memory, not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports one rule: report minimal candidate sets, not every superset.

source: Console, Dupre, Torasso (1991) On the relationship between abduction and deduction, J. Logic and Computation 1(5):661-690
finding: Shows abductive diagnosis (explain the symptoms with fault models) and consistency-based diagnosis (do not contradict them) belong to one family. With complete fault models, the consistency-based diagnoses that also entail the observations are the abductive ones. Weaker models leave the consistency form as a superset.
numbers: Formal result, no empirical numbers.
limits: From memory, not opened. Companion: Console and Torasso (1991) A spectrum of logical definitions of model-based diagnosis, Computational Intelligence 7(3).
agent_relevance: Tells us which test to use: if we have a fault story for each suspect, require it to entail the failing output; if not, only require no contradiction.

source: Bylander, Allemang, Tanner, Josephson (1991) The computational complexity of abduction, Artificial Intelligence 49:25-60
finding: Shows that finding a best explanation is NP-hard in the general set-cover setting, and that finding a minimal-cardinality cover is hard to approximate well. Special cases with independent, non-interacting causes are easier.
numbers: Complexity result only; no empirical numbers (from memory).
limits: From memory, not opened.
agent_relevance: Justifies a hard budget and code-side search: do not ask the model to enumerate all explanations.

source: Peng and Reggia (1990) Abductive Inference Models for Diagnostic Problem-Solving, Springer; Reggia, Nau, Wang (1983) parsimonious covering
finding: Parsimonious covering theory: a diagnosis is a set of disorders that covers all findings and is irredundant or minimal. A probabilistic extension ranks covers. Applied in diagnostic systems for internal medicine.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: From memory, not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives the cover-and-minimality view for S5: every observation must be covered by some suspect.

source: Josephson and Josephson (1994) Abductive Inference: Computation, Philosophy, Technology, Cambridge UP
finding: Frames abduction as inference to the best explanation. Cited by the Wikipedia page for the claim that fault detection is the most direct application of abduction.
numbers: Verified only that Wikipedia cites it with ISBN 978-0521434614.
limits: Book not opened; secondary mention only.
agent_relevance: Best explanation needs comparison with rivals; the scaffold should list at least two rival causes before accepting one.

source: Steiglechner, Mahler, Lohmann (2026) LLMs Can See the Smoke but not the Fire: Evaluating Abductive Reasoning with Elenchos
finding: Generative test of abduction as a structural inverse problem. A reference formal system and a possibly mutated copy are given under black-box probing. The agent must say if a mutation exists and which rule changes cause the behaviour difference. Models detect that something changed far more often than they find what changed.
numbers: 13 LLMs in the Ladder experiment, averaged over k in {1,2} and prompt levels: detection accuracy 0.65 versus exact attribution accuracy 0.28. Hardest cell (minimal prompt, interacting mutations): average accuracy 0.02. Random baselines 1/13 = 0.077 (k=1), 1/64 = 0.016 (k=2), 1/3 for kernel choice.
limits: Preprint, July 2026. Synthetic rule systems, not real devices. Compute finding is labelled preliminary by the authors.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that something is wrong and which part is wrong are separate skills. The fault-location step must be done by code from real failing outputs (G2), not by the model's sense of the cause.

source: Elenchos wide-panel benchmark: multi-mutation collapse
finding: Across 30 LLMs, exact accuracy falls sharply as the number of hidden faults grows. Interacting faults almost wipe out success. Models stop after one plausible explanation.
numbers: Average exact accuracy 0.90, 0.32, 0.15, 0.15 for k = 0, 1, 2+, 3+ mutations. Interacting set 0.03. Jaccard similarity lowest at k=2 (0.27). Failures dominated by under-reporting rather than invented mutations.
limits: 30-model panel under one fixed baseline configuration.
agent_relevance: Single-fault bias is a known failure. Rule: after a cause explains part of the evidence, code checks the residual (unexplained observations) and reopens search if any remain.

source: Elenchos: premature commitment and telling the model the fault count
finding: In 86.5 percent of runs where the model found the corrupt part but failed to name the exact mutation, the probe budget was left unused. So failures happen before the budget runs out. Telling the model k pushes it to invent mutations to fill slots; not telling it makes it omit them.
numbers: 86.5 percent of (detected, wrong attribution) cases had unused probe budget. With k known, hallucinated mutations rise; with k unknown, omissions rise (Supplementary Table 9).
limits: Conditioned on correct kernel detection and k=2.
agent_relevance: Do not give the model a target count of faults. Let a residual check, not a quota, decide whether to keep looking (supports G1).

source: Elenchos: scaffolding and inference-time compute
finding: More structural information in the system prompt (Level 0) gives large gains over Levels 1 and 2, and weak models fail almost entirely without it. Moving from low to high reasoning effort gave no statistically significant gain in attribution accuracy in preliminary tests. At k=2, Level-2 prompt, interacting mutations, most models failed completely; only gpt-5.4_medium (0.20) and gpt-5.4 (0.07) scored above 0, and the highest reasoning-budget setting scored 0.
numbers: gpt-5.4_medium 0.20; gpt-5.4 0.07; highest-budget setting 0.00 in that cell.
limits: Authors say the compute finding needs larger-scale validation.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the model an explicit system description in the scaffold over simply asking for longer thinking.

source: Mohiuddin, Kranti, Hakimov, Schlangen (2026) Don't Let Me Ask for It: active multi-turn information acquisition for abductive inference (Alien Abduction game)
finding: Model must infer a hidden Python function from input-output evidence under four modes: evidence upfront versus over turns, and queries chosen by the model versus by an oracle. Success is higher when evidence is handed over than when the model has to ask for it. Models also do better with oracle examples than with their own queries.
numbers: Overall success rates range from 0.03 (Qwen3.6-35B) through 0.20 (Mistral-Large-3) to 0.64 (GPT5.4). Turn budget 15. Order for most models: single-turn > passive > active. Qwen3.6-35B had parser errors in 40.64 percent of instances.
limits: Hidden functions are small Python functions in five domains. Format-following failures confound one model.
agent_relevance: Choosing the next test is a weak step for models. In S7 the program, not the model, should pick the next probe that separates surviving hypotheses.

source: Alien Abduction: hypothesis retrodiction accuracy and stopping
finding: Hypothesis retrodiction accuracy (HRA) is the share of observed evidence that the model's current hypothesis reproduces. Some models commit before using the evidence; others use all 15 turns without converging. Models form hypotheses that fit self-picked evidence without separating them from rivals.
numbers: HRA = matched evidence / observed evidence at turn t; a belief-tracking agent should stay at 1. Final-turn HRA is 1.00 for several models and modes and lower in passive-output.
limits: Metric needs a runnable hypothesis; fits program-like targets, not open diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Cheap code check for G2/G3: re-run the candidate cause against every observation seen so far and count mismatches. Require zero before stopping.

source: Luo et al. (2026, ICML) Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models
finding: Names four failure modes of deductive prompting frameworks on abduction: evidence fabrication, context drift, failed backtracking, early stopping. Proposes a causal graph of hypotheses and evidence plus a state machine with support/refute updates and drill-down thresholds. Nodes must come from real tool returns.
numbers: Human-judge medical diagnosis (DiagnosisArena made interactive): GoS Match 39.86 percent, Relevant 78.99 percent, $0.12 per case. Best baseline Multi/FoT $0.73 per case. Distributed-system failure diagnosis: Match 70.67, Relevant 88.00, $0.10 per case.
limits: Authors' own method and benchmark reformulation. LLM judge scores lower than human judge. Table columns in the PDF text are garbled, so the GoS LLM-judge row is not recorded.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our design: code-held state, evidence from real outputs, support/refute bookkeeping, thresholds for stopping.

source: Graph of States: ablation and error distribution
finding: Removing the causal graph or the state machine costs a lot. A structured notebook without a causal graph helps but stays far below the full method. GoS removes evidence fabrication but backtracking still fails often. Without the state machine the system burns its full budget before concluding.
numbers: Ablation (LLM judge, Match): w/o causal graph 18.12 percent, w/o state machine 12.32 percent; cost rises to $0.17 per case without the state machine. Error shares, baselines pooled versus GoS: evidence fabrication 22.22 vs 0, failed backtracking 52.78 vs 30.90 (text confirms 0 vs 22.22 and 30.90); context drift and early stopping cells parsed from a garbled table, treat as approximate.
limits: Some ablation cells could not be aligned reliably.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the bookkeeping structure, not extra sampling, gives the gain. Supports code-held hypothesis and evidence lists.

source: Gao et al. (2026) One Hypothesis Is Not Enough: HypoAgent, abductive reasoning over knowledge graphs
finding: Abduction over a knowledge graph means finding a logic formula whose answer set matches observed entities. One-shot generators cannot detect mismatches. HypoAgent adds root-cause analysis using fragment-level coverage, then refines. A plain ReAct LLM with KG tools is worse than symbolic search.
numbers: Single-turn Jaccard on BioKG: symbolic search 0.420, ReAct 0.224, CtrlHGen 0.718, CtrlHGen best-of-k 0.758, HypoAgent 0.885 (DeepSeek), 0.859 (Qwen), 0.860 (GPT). DBpedia50 Jaccard: CtrlHGen 0.781, HypoAgent 0.945 (DeepSeek).
limits: A small trained generator proposes; the LLM refines. Knowledge-graph hypotheses, not physical systems.
agent_relevance: Gains beat best-of-k, so they come from diagnosing the mismatch, not extra samples. Supports: compute which part of the hypothesis fails to cover, show that part to the model, let it revise (G2).

source: Abe et al. (2026) Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models
finding: Converted a syllogism dataset into abduction (infer the minor premise from rule and conclusion). Models show belief bias and negation bias. Items whose right answer is Neither are very hard; models often treat the task as deduction.
numbers: Zero-shot GPT-4 abduction accuracy about 42 percent, slightly above chance; over 80 percent on Positive and Negative items, poor on Neither. Inconsistent-content items about 10 points lower. Few-shot: Llama-3-70B 75.46 percent abduction vs 84.72 deduction. GPT-4 deduction 72.22 zero-shot, 95.83 few-shot. GPT-4 picks Negative 67.90 percent when negation appears, true rate 16.67 percent. Against deduction labels GPT-4 agrees 51.85 percent overall, 8.33 percent on Neither.
limits: Small dataset of syllogism forms; older models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-3).
agent_relevance: Models often answer the forward question instead of the backward one. Fix: force the explicit step of stating what the model predicts, then compare.

source: Arthur (2026) Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
finding: 120 people did 160 forced-choice aNLI items. Reasoning token counts of large reasoning models correlate with human reaction time even after controlling for item length. Items a model gets wrong are items humans also get wrong more often.
numbers: N = 120, 160 items, mean human accuracy 78.8 percent. Partial correlations tokens vs RT: GPT-OSS-120B r = 0.552, GPT-OSS-20B 0.41, Qwen3-235B-Thinking 0.359, DeepSeek-R1 0.327, Kimi-K2-Thinking 0.303, GLM-4.5-Air 0.263, Qwen3-32B-Thinking 0.229, DeepSeek-V3 (non-reasoning) 0.197. Human accuracy 82.5 percent on items R1 got right vs 47.8 percent on items R1 got wrong (r = 0.53).
limits: Short commonsense items; correlation, not causation; tests effort alignment, not explanation quality.
agent_relevance: Hard abductive items cost both humans and models more. Token count may serve as a cheap difficulty hint for the impasse detector, never as proof.

source: Quan, Xiong, Valentino, Freitas (2026) Inferring Latent Intentions: Attributional NLI in LLM Agents (Att-NLI, Undercover-V)
finding: Agents that combine abductive hypotheses about hidden intent with deductive verification by an external theorem prover beat pure-deduction and abduction-only LLM agents in a social deduction game.
numbers: Neuro-symbolic abductive-deductive agent: average spy win rate 17.08 percent, top of a clear hierarchy of three agent types.
limits: Game with hidden roles; small absolute win rates; abstract and metric sections read, not every table.
agent_relevance: Separate the guess step (model) from the verify step (symbolic checker), the same split as G3.

source: Salimi et al. (2026) Wiring the Why: A Unified Taxonomy and Survey of Abductive Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Survey with a benchmark suite of two stages: Stage I generate hypotheses, Stage II select among given ones. Selecting is far easier than generating. Among formal tasks, AbductionRules is easy and ProofWriter hard because several single missing facts can fit.
numbers: DDXPlus: strongest model 79.75 percent Top-1 and 98.7 percent Hit@3 when ranking provided candidates, but only 63.0 Hit@3 and 28.1 Set-F1@3 when generating diagnoses itself. Benchmarks covered include ART, e-CARE, UNcommonsense, Sherlock, DDXPlus, MedCaseReasoning, ProofWriter.
limits: Survey authors ran the suite themselves; model names not recorded here. Full-pipeline generate-then-select evaluation is called out as missing.
agent_relevance: Candidate generation is the weak stage. Have code supply a candidate list from the system structure, then let the model rank.

source: Salimi et al. (2026) survey: open gaps
finding: Notes that scoring often ignores explanatory virtues (consistency, parsimony, diversity, predictive usefulness) and names choosing the next diagnostic test or experiment as an open need.
numbers: No single number; passages on parsimony and next-test selection.
limits: Opinion section of a survey.
agent_relevance: Two of our operators, minimal-cause selection and next-test selection, have no standard benchmark.

source: DDx study (Google) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: An LLM tuned for diagnostic reasoning produced differential diagnoses on 302 hard NEJM case reports. Alone it beat unassisted clinicians, and assisted clinicians beat unassisted and search-assisted clinicians.
numbers: 20 clinicians, 302 cases, 2 clinicians per case. LLM alone top-10 accuracy 59.1 percent vs 33.6 percent unassisted clinicians (p = 0.04). Clinicians with LLM 51.7 percent vs 36.1 percent unassisted (McNemar 45.7, p < 0.01) and vs 44.4 percent with search (p = 0.03).
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Top-10 list, not one final answer. NEJM cases are published and may overlap training data.
agent_relevance: A model supplying a ranked candidate list helps people more than raw search, which fits generating suspects then checking them.
